intro: Here is the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, whose story runs from the 4th century BC to AD 401. It was one of the Seven Wonders, yet today a single column, re-erected from fragments, stands in its place. Picture a marble forest 137 metres long, raised on marshy ground. Pliny says 36 of its columns were carved in relief at the base. The model shows the third temple, rebuilt in the 4th century BC.
spot-1: Now you are looking at the cella, the roofed inner room. This is where the cult statue of Artemis stood, at the very heart of the temple.
spot-2: Now you are looking at the place of the sculpted drum. Pliny says thirty-six columns were carved at the base, and one of them is in the British Museum today.
spot-3: Now you are looking at the double colonnade. This is a dipteros: two rows of columns wrap the whole building, 127 in all. Let your eye run along them.
spot-4: Now you are looking up at the gabled roof, with a pediment at either end. In the model, the roof is built up in steps.
uncertainty: Finally, what this model does not know. Only foundations and scattered fragments survive, so the plan is disputed. The sources give the dimensions and Pliny's 127 columns, but not the grid they stood in. The model is laid out to reach 127, yet the spacing, the pitch of the roof and the ornament of the pediment are all inference. And the carved column bases are left plain in the model.
